group.title: Shopping and money
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: The amount of money you must pay for something.
examples: The {price} of bread went up again.
wrong: The price of the bag is blue.

words.meaning: To have a price of a certain amount.
examples: How much does this shirt {cost}?
wrong: The ticket costs nothing, so it is very expensive.

words.meaning: To give money for something you buy.
examples: Can I {pay} by card?
wrong: I paid for the coffee, so the shop gave me money.

words.meaning: To use money to buy things.
examples: I {spend} too much on clothes.
wrong: I spent all my money, so now I have more than before.

words.meaning: To give something to someone for money.
examples: They {sell} fresh fish at the market.
wrong: The shop sells bread, so you can’t buy any there.

words.meaning: A small flat round piece of metal money.
examples: I found a {coin} under the sofa.
wrong: A coin is a paper note that you fold.

words.meaning: The money you get back when you pay too much.
examples: Here is your {change}: two dollars.
wrong: I paid the exact price, so I got a lot of change.

words.meaning: Money in coins and notes, not a card.
examples: Do you have any {cash} for the taxi?
wrong: I paid in cash with my credit card.

words.meaning: A plastic card you use to buy now and pay later.
examples: I paid for the hotel with my {credit card}.
wrong: I pay with a credit card made of coins.

words.meaning: A small flat case for money and cards.
examples: He keeps his cards in his {wallet}.
wrong: I keep my soup in my wallet.

words.meaning: A paper that shows how much you must pay.
examples: Can we have the {bill}, please?
wrong: The waiter brought the bill before we ordered.

words.meaning: A time when a shop sells things at lower prices.
examples: I bought these shoes in the {sale}.
wrong: Everything costs more in the sale.

words.meaning: The activity of going to shops to buy things.
examples: We do our {shopping} on Saturday.
wrong: I went shopping, but I never visited a shop.

words.meaning: How big or small something is.
examples: What {size} are your shoes?
wrong: This shirt is the wrong size, so it fits perfectly.

words.meaning: To put on clothes to see if they fit.
examples: Can I {try on} this jacket?
wrong: I tried on the soup to see if it fit.

words.meaning: To be the right size for someone.
examples: These jeans don’t {fit} me.
wrong: The shoes fit well, so they hurt my feet.

words.meaning: To take something back to the shop.
examples: I want to {return} this broken phone.
wrong: I returned the shirt, so I still have it.

words.meaning: A line of people waiting for something.
examples: There was a long {queue} at the bank.
wrong: There was a queue, so nobody was waiting.

words.meaning: A person who helps customers in a shop.
examples: The {shop assistant} found my size.
wrong: The shop assistant is the person who buys everything in the shop.

words.meaning: A small bag for money and cards.
examples: She took a coin out of her {purse}.
wrong: I keep my car in my purse.

words.meaning: Something you buy for less than it is worth.
examples: This coat was a {bargain} at ten dollars.
wrong: It was a bargain because it cost twice the usual price.

words.meaning: A small piece of paper or cloth that gives information about a thing.
examples: Read the {label} before you wash it.
wrong: A label is a kind of pocket.

words.meaning: A long flat surface in a shop where you pay.
examples: Please pay at the {counter}.
wrong: I sleep on the counter in my bedroom.

words.meaning: A metal basket on wheels that you push in a supermarket.
examples: Put the bags in the {trolley}.
wrong: I drink coffee from a trolley.

words.meaning: A container for carrying things, often with a handle.
examples: She put the apples in her {basket}.
wrong: A basket is a kind of hat that you eat.

words.meaning: Without spending much money.
examples: You can eat {cheaply} in this town.
wrong: We lived cheaply, so we spent all our money.

words.meaning: To have enough money to buy something.
examples: We can’t {afford} a new car.
wrong: I can afford it, so I don’t have enough money.

words.meaning: To give something to someone for a short time.
examples: Can you {lend} me your bike?
wrong: I lent him money, so he never has to give it back.

words.meaning: To need to pay money back to someone.
examples: I {owe} you ten dollars.
wrong: I owe him money, so he must pay me.

words.meaning: A piece of paper money.
examples: She paid with a twenty-dollar {note}.
wrong: A note is a metal coin.

words.meaning: A large shop that sells many kinds of things.
examples: We bought a bed at the {department store}.
wrong: A department store is a tiny shop that sells only stamps.

words.meaning: Ready for customers to come in.
examples: Is the shop {open} on Sunday?
wrong: The shop is open, so we can’t go in.

words.meaning: Not open for customers.
examples: The bank is {closed} today.
wrong: The shop is closed, so let’s go in and buy bread.

words.meaning: The whole amount after you add everything.
examples: The {total} is forty dollars.
wrong: The total is smaller than each of the prices.

words.meaning: Money that a shop gives back to you.
examples: I asked for a {refund} for the broken lamp.
wrong: A refund is money you pay twice for the same thing.

words.meaning: Money that parents give to children each week.
examples: She saves her {pocket money} for books.
wrong: Pocket money is the salary a manager gets.

words.meaning: To bring goods to a person’s home or office.
examples: They {deliver} the pizza in thirty minutes.
wrong: They delivered the sofa, so it is still in the shop.

words.meaning: The goods a shop has to sell.
examples: Sorry, that phone is out of {stock}.
wrong: It is in stock, so the shop has none.

words.meaning: The place in a supermarket where you pay.
examples: The {checkout} was very busy.
wrong: The checkout is where you choose your vegetables.

words.meaning: Having a value of a certain amount.
examples: This old coin is {worth} a lot of money.
wrong: The car is worth nothing, so people pay a lot for it.
